newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: World Bank calls for Slovak accounting upgrade.
newsitem.headline: World Bank calls for Slovak accounting upgrade.

text.p: Slovakia should introduce international accounting and auditing standards to enable better central bank supervision over the banking sector, the World Bank (WB) said.

In a report on Slovakia made available to Reuters, the WB said that stability of the domestic banking system depended on a reduction of the lending activities of state-controlled banks with the state keeping only a regulatory role.
The WB said that while banking legislation had been amended recently to improve central bank supervision over the sector and main regulations were in place, two key issues were still outstanding.
"First, accounting and auditing systems in both banks and enterprises have not kept pace with the requirements of a market economy," the report said.
"A common set of accounting standards consistent with IAS (international accounting standards) would have to be developed," it added.

The second problem, the WB said, is that personal skills of NBS employees should be upgraded to deal with the increasing diversity and complexity of financial instruments and globalisation of financial markets.

The WB said that while the long-term goal was the development of a competitive and stable banking system dominated by private institutions, the short-term goal should be a reduction of lending activities of state-controlled commercial banks.
"This means that the existing private banks would be the main sources of new lending until the state-controlled banks are privatised," the report said.

At present, the three major financial institutions, commercial banks VUB and IRB and the largest savings bank, Slovenska Sporitelna, are still controlled by the state and account for more than two-thirds of the total volume of loans in Slovakia.
VUB, alone, accounts for some 33 percent of the total.
Small, fully private banks meanwhile have increased their share of loans to about 31 percent this year -- mainly to private sector clients -- from only 11 percent in 1992.
